summary: An implementor's guide for the Internet Printing Protocol version 1.1, one of a set of documents describing IPP.

eli5.summary: It's a how-to helper for people building programs that talk to printers.

questions: what is the internet printing protocol
what is the ipp implementors guide
subtitle: Practical advice for building IPP/1.1 clients and printers: request checking, job validation, character sets and HTTP transport.

tldr.problem: The IPP/1.1 specifications leave many details open, and interoperability testing events kept turning up places where implementations disagreed.
tldr.mechanism: This guide supplements the Model and Semantics and the Encoding and Transport documents. It suggests the order of checks an IPP object can run on a request, an algorithm for validating job attributes, and clarifications on character sets, directories, security and HTTP use.
tldr.outcome: It is not part of the formal specification, and the base documents win in any conflict. It is Informational and obsoletes RFC 2639, the guide for IPP/1.0.

today: RFC 3196 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 2639. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Place in the IPP Document Set
sections.content:
The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) is an application-level protocol for distributed printing. This Implementor's Guide supplements the IPP Model and Semantics (RFC 2911) and the IPP Transport and Encoding (RFC 2910). It helps implementers of both IPP/1.1 and IPP/1.0, gives a typical order of processing requests, and explains the motivation for some decisions. It obsoletes RFC 2639, the guide for IPP/1.0.

The guide is not part of the formal specification. If it contradicts RFC 2911 or RFC 2910, those documents take precedence. Its sections parallel the numbering of the Model document so they are easy to cross-reference.

Many items are "issues" raised at three interoperability testing events, held in September 1998, March 1999 and October 2000. Issues from the first two have been folded into the base documents but their discussion is kept here.
sections.eli5: It is a helper booklet beside the real rulebook. If the booklet and the rulebook ever disagree, the rulebook wins.

sections.title: Suggested Request Processing Steps
sections.content:
Section 3.1.2 suggests the steps and error checks an IPP object may perform. An implementation can be "strict" and do all of them, or "forgiving" and accept requests from non-conforming clients. Because of this, status codes can differ between implementations and a client SHOULD NOT expect exactly the codes described. A client MUST still send requests that would pass every check. The guide also says clients SHOULD use Validate-Job before sending a large document, since a status code may only arrive after all the data is sent.

The checks run in order: validate the version, the operation identifier, the presence and order of attribute groups, and the presence and values of the required Operation attributes, then the optional ones. A wrong version gives server-error-version-not-supported and an unknown operation gives server-error-operation-not-supported. Missing or out-of-order groups give client-error-bad-request.

Unknown attribute groups in the expected position, just before the document content, are ignored rather than rejected, because they may come from a later minor version. The charset, natural language and target attributes MUST come first, in that order.

For versions, a printer must reply with the nearest version it supports. If the client's exact minor version is supported, the printer MUST respond with that same version.
sections.eli5: It is a checklist a printer can follow when a request arrives: is the language right, is the job well-formed, is every part filled in. A strict printer checks everything and a forgiving one lets small mistakes slide.

sections.title: Validating Jobs and Job Lifecycle
sections.content:
To check a Job Template attribute xxx against the Printer's xxx-supported attribute, the guide gives a small algorithm. Each value of a multi-valued request attribute is checked separately, and a value passes if it matches any supported value. An integer is valid if it is within a supported range, a URI if its scheme matches, and anything else if the types are equal and the values equal. Unsupported attributes and values are copied to the Unsupported Attributes group of the response. Whether the request is then rejected depends on ipp-attribute-fidelity.

After a job is created, the Printer schedules it by its own algorithms, moves it to processing, and then to completed. A Cancel-Job eventually gives canceled, and an unrecoverable error gives aborted. When the job object is later destroyed, requests for it return client-error-not-found or client-error-gone. The Printer SHOULD NOT reuse a job-uri or job-id for a long time, so stale client references do not hit a newer job.
sections.eli5: For every setting you ask for, the printer checks whether it offers it. Anything it cannot do gets listed in the reply so you know. After that, a job goes from waiting to printing to finished.

sections.title: Character Sets and Printing Edge Cases
sections.content:
IPP clients and objects are REQUIRED to support UTF-8 and may support more. It is RECOMMENDED that an IPP object also support US-ASCII, and list utf-8 and us-ascii in its charsets-supported. An object that supports both MUST accept a request in either, convert between them with the highest fidelity possible, and return successful-ok rather than a warning.

Other clarifications cover practical cases. A paused or stalled printer may flow-control the data of a Print-Job at the TCP layer, so it should not return an error response in that state. A server that forwards jobs to a device without job status can answer completed, pending with job-outgoing, or the out-of-band unknown for the job state. For a Printer that has a DNS name, the printer-uri-supported attribute may hold the name, the IP address, or both, as the administrator configures.
sections.eli5: Every printer and computer must at least understand one common alphabet, UTF-8, and it helps if they also know plain ASCII. A busy printer may simply make you wait instead of saying no.

sections.title: Encoding, HTTP Transport and Long Waits
sections.content:
IPP runs on HTTP. HTTP/1.1 MUST be supported by all clients and servers, and HTTP/1.0 is an optional extra for talking to non-conforming peers. A server need not reply until it has the whole request, but it is recommended to send an error as soon as it detects one. A client that is chunking can then send a premature zero-length chunk to end the request and keep the connection open.

IPP uses TCP flow control to throttle clients when printers are busy, so a client may be blocked for a very long time. Socket timeouts must be avoided, and a client should set an infinite timeout while it sends a job. A client can open another connection and use Get-Printer-Attributes to learn why it is blocked, for instance a jam or no paper.

The guide has tables of HTTP headers for clients and servers. For example Transfer-Encoding may only be chunked and MUST be present if Content-Length is absent. Chunked requests are REQUIRED of IPP Printers because some HTTP/1.1 servers accept chunked responses but reject chunked POST requests with a 411 or 413 status code.
sections.eli5: A printer that is jammed may not answer for a long time, so the sender must be patient. The sender can also ask a second question on a new line, like "what is wrong", while the first job waits.

sections.title: Security Notes
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 2911 section 8 all apply. The guide adds one clarification from testing, issue 1.32, about jobs submitted by other protocols. A device that accepts such "foreign" jobs should at least let them be queried with Get-Jobs, returning job-id and job-uri as unknown, and should generate those values where possible.

It also says how to treat ownership. Foreign jobs could belong to other users, or to anonymous, and only an authenticated operator or administrator could query them, unless the security policy lets users see other users' jobs. The guide also assumes that authentication and authorization have already taken place at a lower layer.
sections.eli5: If jobs can reach the printer by some other route, they still need a rule about who is allowed to see them.
